text: Hello everybody, welcome back.In the previous lesson, we identified the pros and cons of eternal life and recognized the author's attitude towards immortality.Today, in the second period of this unit, we'll read the passage more carefully to see how the author constructs the arguments.First of all, let's take a quick look at the objectives today.By the end of this period, you are expected to probe deeper into the passage of From here to eternity to form and clearly express your opinion on the idea of immortality.And you are also expected to make your arguments about immortality and whether to be drawn again more convincing by practicing the method of argumentation you learn in this lesson.These are the materials required for this period of learning.Please make sure your textbook and worksheet are at hand.Before we dig deeper into the passage of From here to eternity, let's first refresh our memory on what we've learned.What do you know about Dmitry Itzkov's immortality project?Yes, it was founded by Dmitry Itzkov, a media entrepreneur, and it aims to transplant a human mind into a robot body in the near future.Eventually, the project claims to have the potential to free the majority of all people on the planet from disease, old age, and even death.What are the pros and cons of immortality listed in the passage?Yes, as you can recall from the previous lesson, these are the pros and cons the writer mentions.Is the writer in favor of or against the idea of immortality?He is against the idea.Even though he does mention some pros of eternal life, he refutes them as incorrect understanding of immortality.And so in the end, he concludes, by accepting that life is limited and cannot be sustained indefinitely, we are able to give more value to the time we have and to think carefully about how we are using it and what we hope to achieve, because we might not get another chance.What is your opinion of immortality?Of course, there is no standard answer.But whatever your opinion is, we'll have to learn to make your argument stronger and more persuasive.And there's a lot we can learn from this passage.Let's take paragraph 5 as an example.In this paragraph, the writer first makes the point that immortality would influence how society develops and progresses, but merely stating that is not convincing enough.And therefore, in the next sentence, the writer makes clear how immortality would influence the development and progress of a society.And he also writes about the consequence that society would become less dynamic.But the writer doesn't stop here.Instead, he elaborates on his point by presenting an imaginary world of immortality for all of people from the 18th century.As we read on, we further understand why, as the population grew older in an immortal world, there would be more resistance to progress.In the end, the writer cites a quotation from a famous scientist to clarify how society normally develops, and further explains how immortal old people will slow down the development of society.Also, by providing the name and reputation of Planck as Nobel physicist and the father of quantum mechanics, the writer adds waste to his argument and convinces us that he is telling the truth.In a word, the writer provides us with plenty of relevant supporting information such as what, why, and how, etc., and thus makes his points more persuasive.You've all picked your side at the beginning of the lesson when I asked your opinion on the idea of immortality, haven't you?Now, let's try to add some relevant supporting information by using the techniques learned to make your opinions more convincing.If you are for the idea of immortality, you may argue that with eternal life, people could explore endless possibilities.If you are against the idea, it is very likely that you will argue that in an immortal world, the population would put pressure on our already limited global resources.But apparently, these two arguments are not well developed.With regard to these two arguments, can you raise some relevant follow-up questions?For example, for the first argument, I would like to ask, what could the endless possibilities be?It's your turn now.Please raise at least two WH questions for each argument.You'll be given two minutes to prepare.Thank you for watching.If you like this video, please give it a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel.See you next time.What questions did you raise?These questions are just for your reference.For the first argument, my follow-up questions would be, what could the endless possibilities be?How can these endless possibilities benefit us human beings?Are these endless possibilities good for us?And what could the consequences be without these endless possibilities?For the second argument, I would ask, why would overpopulation put pressure on our resources?What kinds of resources would run out?What could the consequences be if these resources run out?Of course, you can raise more questions.By answering these questions, you are sure to make those arguments well-developed.Now it is your turn.Please write down a short paragraph on your worksheet
